q: An insulin pump creates all its tasks, queues and timers at boot and never deletes anything. The safety standard bans dynamic allocation after init. Which heap fits best?
options: heap_1
heap_3
heap_4
heap_5
explain: **heap_1** is a deterministic bump allocator that never frees. That's exactly "allocate at boot, keep forever", and it can't fragment. Better still is full static allocation (`xTaskCreateStatic`) with dynamic allocation disabled. heap_3 wraps the non-deterministic libc `malloc`. heap_4 and heap_5 add free and coalescing that this design never needs, which is more code to certify.

q: After a full worst-case test campaign, `uxTaskGetStackHighWaterMark(comms_handle)` returns **12**. What does that mean?
options: The comms task used 12 words of stack at most
At its worst moment so far, comms had only 12 words (48 bytes) of stack left unused, which is dangerously tight
Comms overflowed its stack 12 times
12% of the stack is in use
explain: The high-water mark is the **minimum free stack ever**, in words, found by checking how much of the 0xA5 fill pattern is still untouched. 12 words means one deeper call path, a bigger local or an extra exception frame could overflow it. Grow the stack until there's comfortable headroom (often 20–30%). It's a free amount, not a usage figure, a count or a percentage.

options: Method 1 checks the stack pointer at context switches
Method 2 also checks that the stack's last bytes still hold the fill pattern
Either method guarantees an overflow is caught before any memory is corrupted
When it detects one, it calls vApplicationStackOverflowHook()
explain: Both methods run **at a context switch**, so they detect an overflow *after* it happened. By then a neighbouring TCB or stack may already be corrupted, which is why C is false. Method 2's pattern check catches overflows that unwound before the switch, which Method 1 misses. Both call your hook with the task's handle and name. For prevention rather than detection, use an MPU guard region or Armv8-M's stack-limit registers.

q: Why does `xTaskCreateStatic` help capacity planning compared with `xTaskCreate`?
options: Static tasks run faster
The stack and TCB are ordinary arrays, so the linker fails the build if RAM is over-committed instead of the product failing at runtime
Static tasks can't overflow their stacks
It allows priorities above configMAX_PRIORITIES
explain: With static allocation, every byte is a named variable in `.bss`, so the **linker** adds it all up and errors out if it doesn't fit. Runtime `NULL`s from an exhausted heap disappear. Speed is the same once a task is created, the stack can overflow just as easily, so you still measure the high-water mark, and priorities are unaffected.

q: A design kicks the hardware watchdog from the SysTick interrupt. The throttle task deadlocks, but the car doesn't reset. What's the design flaw?
options: The watchdog timeout is too long
SysTick keeps running even when tasks are dead, so the watchdog only proves the timer interrupt works, not that the critical tasks are healthy
Hardware watchdogs can't detect deadlocks
SysTick has too low an interrupt priority
explain: A watchdog is only as good as the evidence used to kick it. Kick it only when **every critical task has checked in** within its deadline. A supervisor that collects check-ins does this (you'll build one in the boss). Then a dead or stuck task stops the kicks and the hardware resets into a safe state. A shorter timeout or a different IRQ priority doesn't fix a kick that's independent of task health.
